meta.title: Spain · The 211 Files
meta.description: Spain profile in The 211 Files: country, federation, origins, competitions, national-team history, clubs, stadiums and its place at the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

hero.title: Spain
hero.subtitle: The reigning world champions enter the road to the Centennial World Cup with their place already secured — not through qualification, but as one of the tournament’s six hosts.

sections.title: Spain at a glance
paragraphs: Spain occupies most of the Iberian Peninsula and includes the Balearic and Canary Islands, plus Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa. A diverse country of around 49 million people, it blends distinct regional identities, languages and cultures under a constitutional monarchy.

Its twentieth century was marked by the end of the Restoration system, the Second Republic, a devastating Civil War and almost four decades of dictatorship. Democracy was restored through the 1978 Constitution, after which Spain rapidly integrated with its European neighbours.
Today it is one of the European Union’s largest economies and labour markets, as well as a major global centre of culture, tourism and sport.

sections.title: The RFEF
sections.intro: The national governing body sits above a broad territorial structure that reflects Spain’s regional diversity.
paragraphs: The Federación Española de Clubs de Football was created in 1909. Reorganisation followed during a turbulent early period, and the federation received the title “Real” from King Alfonso XIII in 1913.

The RFEF brings together the regional federations, clubs, players, referees, coaches and the professional league. It governs Spain’s national teams and the principal national cup competitions, while the professional league operates the top two men’s divisions.

sections.title: From British enclaves to a national sport

items.title: Football reaches Spain
items.text: British workers, engineers and sailors introduced football in several ports and industrial enclaves. The Río Tinto mining community and nearby Huelva became one of the game’s most important early centres.

items.title: The oldest surviving club
items.text: British residents founded Huelva Recreation Club, today’s Recreativo de Huelva and the oldest surviving football club in Spain.

items.title: The first documented formal match
items.text: A Sevilla side beat Huelva 2–0 in what is generally treated as Spain’s first documented formal football match.

items.title: The major clubs emerge
items.text: Football quickly took root among locals. Athletic Club emerged in Bilbao in 1898, FC Barcelona in 1899 and Madrid FC in 1902.

items.title: From regional cups to a national championship
items.text: The Copa Macaya became an early regional landmark. The 1902 Copa de la Coronación then inspired the Copa del Rey, first contested as Spain’s national championship in 1903.

items.title: A national federation
items.text: The Spanish federation was constituted, bringing a national layer of organisation to a game that had previously developed through clubs and regional bodies.

cards.title: La Liga
cards.text: Professionalism was regulated in 1926. Three years later the national league began, with Barcelona becoming its first champion. The top flight developed into one of world football’s most influential competitions.

cards.title: Copa del Rey
cards.text: Spain’s oldest nationwide competition grew from the early championship organised after the Copa de la Coronación. Its open knockout format has linked clubs from different levels for more than a century.

cards.title: Regional foundations
cards.text: Before a stable national structure existed, regional championships organised the game. Their legacy survives in the autonomous federations that remain a central part of the RFEF system.

items.title: A team created for Antwerp
items.text: Spain assembled its first national team for the Antwerp Olympics. It debuted by beating Denmark 1–0 and ultimately won silver after further victories over Sweden, Italy and the Netherlands.

items.title: Italy take revenge
items.text: Four years after Antwerp, Italy eliminated Spain in the opening round of the Paris Olympics through a Spanish own goal.

items.title: A heavy Amsterdam exit
items.text: Spain opened by defeating Mexico 7–1. A 1–1 quarter-final draw with Italy forced a replay, in which the Italians won 7–1.

items.title: World Cup debut
items.text: Spain beat Brazil 3–1, then held host nation Italy 1–1 after extra time. With no penalty shoot-outs, the quarter-final was replayed the next day and Italy won 1–0.

items.title: Football divided by war
items.text: The Civil War stopped the league and national cup, divided clubs and drove players into exile. Nationwide competition resumed in 1939.

items.title: Fourth in the world
items.text: At the World Cup in Brazil, Telmo Zarra’s goal defeated England at the Maracanã. Spain finished fourth, its best World Cup result for the next sixty years.

items.title: The first senior title
items.text: Spain won the European Championship on home soil. Marcelino’s late header sealed a 2–1 final victory over the Soviet Union in Madrid.

items.title: Real Madrid’s first European dynasty
items.text: Real Madrid transformed Spanish club football by winning the first five European Cups. Alfredo Di Stéfano scored in every final, and the 7–3 victory over Eintracht Frankfurt became the dynasty’s defining performance.

items.title: Barcelona reach the summit
items.text: FC Barcelona won its first European Cup at Wembley, adding a new landmark to a year in which Spain also claimed Olympic football gold in Barcelona.

items.title: Success spreads
items.text: Real Madrid and Barcelona remained global giants, while Valencia, Deportivo, Sevilla and other Spanish clubs reached or won major European finals.

items.title: Sustained continental dominance
items.text: Spanish clubs built an exceptional record in UEFA competitions, combining the financial and global reach of the largest institutions with repeated breakthroughs by clubs from across the country.

sections.title: Hosts, near misses and repeated frustration

items.title: World Cup hosts
items.text: Spain staged the first 24-team World Cup but struggled under the weight of expectation and exited in the second group phase.

items.title: Back in a major final
items.text: Miguel Muñoz’s side reached the European Championship final, where hosts France won 2–0 in Paris.

items.title: Olympic gold in Barcelona
items.text: Spain won the Olympic football tournament at home, defeating Poland 3–2 in the final at Camp Nou.

items.title: A quarter-final stopped by Italy
items.text: Spain advanced unbeaten from its group, defeated Switzerland 3–0 and then lost 2–1 to Italy in the quarter-finals.

items.title: Wembley penalty defeat
items.text: Spain reached the European Championship quarter-finals without losing in normal time, but England eliminated them in a penalty shoot-out.

items.title: A spectacular but futile finale
items.text: A defeat by Nigeria and a draw with Paraguay left Spain dependent on other results. A 6–1 victory over Bulgaria was not enough to avoid a group-stage exit.

items.title: Drama before another French barrier
items.text: Spain recovered from an opening loss to Norway, then beat Yugoslavia 4–3 in a remarkable finish. France ended the run in the quarter-finals.

items.title: The Korean shoot-out
items.text: Spain won all three group matches and eliminated the Republic of Ireland on penalties, but co-hosts South Korea defeated them in another shoot-out after a controversial quarter-final.

items.title: Two more early exits
items.text: Spain went out in the EURO 2004 group stage and, after winning its group at the 2006 World Cup, lost 3–1 to France in the round of 16.

sections.title: From perennial outsiders to serial champions

items.title: The barrier finally falls
items.text: Spain won every group match, survived an Italian penalty shoot-out and defeated Russia in the semi-final. Fernando Torres scored the only goal against Germany to deliver the European title.

items.title: World champions for the first time
items.text: After a shock opening defeat by Switzerland, Spain recovered to win its group. Four consecutive 1–0 knockout victories culminated in Andrés Iniesta’s extra-time goal against the Netherlands.

items.title: Three major titles in succession
items.text: Spain completed an unprecedented men’s cycle by defeating Italy 4–0 in the EURO final — the largest winning margin in the competition’s final.

items.title: The champions collapse
items.text: Heavy defeats by the Netherlands and Chile eliminated Spain before its final group match, bringing the dominant 2008–12 cycle to an abrupt end.

items.title: Knockout frustration returns
items.text: Italy eliminated Spain in the EURO 2016 round of 16. At the 2018 World Cup, the hosts Russia did the same through a penalty shoot-out.

items.title: A young side comes close
items.text: Spain reached the EURO 2020 semi-finals and the 2021 Nations League final, but lost both. Morocco then eliminated La Roja on penalties in the 2022 World Cup round of 16.

items.title: Nations League champions
items.text: Spain defeated Croatia on penalties to win its first UEFA Nations League and its first senior men’s title in eleven years.

items.title: A record fourth EURO
items.text: Spain won all seven matches, defeating Croatia, Italy, Germany, France and England on the way to a record fourth European title.

items.title: Nations League runners-up
items.text: Spain returned to the final but Portugal prevailed in a penalty shoot-out after a 2–2 draw.

items.title: The second star
items.text: Spain began with a 0–0 draw against Cabo Verde, then beat Saudi Arabia 4–0 and Uruguay 1–0 to top Group H. The run ended with Ferran Torres scoring in extra time to defeat Argentina 1–0 in the final.

items.title: FIFA World Cup
items.text: Champions: 2010 and 2026.

items.title: UEFA Nations League
items.text: Champions: 2023. Runners-up: 2021 and 2025.

items.title: Women’s World Cup
items.text: Champions: 2023.

items.title: Women’s Nations League
items.text: Champions: 2024.

items.title: Futsal World Cup
items.text: Men’s champions: 2000 and 2004.

items.title: Current distinction
items.text: Reigning men’s world champions and already qualified for 2030 as hosts.

items.title: Official senior debut
items.text: After years outside the formal federation structure, Spain’s women played their first officially recognised senior international.

items.title: First major tournament
items.text: Spain reached the European Championship semi-finals in its first appearance at a senior women’s finals.

items.title: World Cup debut
items.text: La Roja appeared at the Women’s World Cup for the first time, beginning a rapid rise through the international hierarchy.

items.title: World champions
items.text: Spain defeated England 1–0 in Sydney to win the Women’s World Cup, its first senior women’s global title.

items.title: Nations League and Olympic breakthrough
items.text: Spain won the inaugural UEFA Women’s Nations League and made its first appearance in the women’s Olympic football tournament.

cards.title: Santiago Bernabéu
cards.text: Real Madrid’s home is one of world football’s best-known stadiums. Its extensive redevelopment added a retractable roof, a retractable pitch and new commercial and event spaces.

cards.title: Camp Nou
cards.text: Opened in 1957, FC Barcelona’s home has long been Europe’s largest football stadium. Its reconstruction is designed to raise capacity and modernise the entire venue.

cards.title: El Molinón
cards.text: Home of Sporting de Gijón, El Molinón is generally recognised as Spain’s oldest football ground still in use. Matches were recorded on the site by 1908.

sections.title: The champions will be at home
sections.quote: Spain will not travel the qualifying road to 2030. As one of the six hosts, La Roja already have their place — and will arrive with the second star on the shirt.
